nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Official plugins live in the shipit GitHub org; shipit installs them on first use and prints the lock line
nodes.body:
**Decided by the user**, in the answer to "How do SSH and Hetzner users get the plugin when it leaves the binary?".

- Official plugins live in the shipit GitHub org: `shipit/shipit-ssh` and `shipit/shipit-hetzner`. Fly and Render follow later.
- A config with `provider: ssh` keeps working. On first use, shipit offers to install `shipit/shipit-ssh`.
- After the install, shipit prints the exact lock file line to commit. CI users paste it once. Then CI never meets a surprise download with no entry in the lock file.
- shipit holds a short built-in list of official provider names. The user's view: this list is ours, not a registry. It does not reopen the decision "No plugin list in v1: a GitHub topic for discovery, install by owner/repo only", because it never holds third-party plugins.

**My inference**, not stated by the user:
- The built-in list can also hold the numeric repo id of each official plugin. Then the first install already has the check from the decision "The lock entry of a GitHub plugin records the numeric repo id; a different id is a hard fail".
- In CI with no lock entry, shipit still stops with an error and prints the same line. CI never installs and approves by itself (decision "Approved credential keys live in the project lock file, next to the pinned version and sha256").

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: SSH upload and remote command move to a shared Go module, shipit-sdk; no plugin calls another plugin in v1
nodes.body:
**Decided by the user**, in the answer to "How does the Hetzner plugin reuse the SSH upload and remote command?".

- The SSH upload and remote command code moves to a Go module named `shipit-sdk`.
- `shipit-ssh` and `shipit-hetzner` both import it. Each plugin stays one static binary.
- **No plugin starts another plugin in v1.** That would break the credential model: shipit must start every plugin, so that it controls the environment, HOME and approved keys.
- A fix to the SSH code needs a release of both plugins. The user accepts this: Renovate opens the update PRs.

Effect: the protocol needs no chaining feature. Third-party authors who deploy over SSH, for example a Coolify plugin, can import `shipit-sdk` too.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: shipit accepts both GoReleaser archive name styles; the docs show only the built-in default
nodes.body:
**Decided by the user**, in the answer to "Which archive names must a plugin release use?".

- shipit reads the archive names in the release's checksums file. It picks the one for its OS and CPU, in either GoReleaser style: `linux` or `Linux`, `amd64` or `x86_64`.
- shipit opens both `tar.gz` and `zip` archives.
- **The author docs show one style only:** GoReleaser's built-in default name. Authors copy the docs. The parser for the `goreleaser init` style is only tolerance.

This replaces the author rule in the decision "shipit plugin install accepts GitHub owner/repo or an HTTPS URL to a checksums file", which said archive names must follow the default. The rest of that decision stays.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: On upgrade, a new checksums hash needs a new version; a new URL host needs re-approval
nodes.body:
**Decided by the user**, in their own answer to "What does shipit check on upgrade for a plugin installed from an HTTPS URL?".

- The pinned checksums hash may change only together with a version bump.
- Same version with a different hash: shipit stops with an error. No flag skips this.
- A URL on a different host: shipit stops with an error until somebody approves it again.

Effect on the lock entry of a URL plugin: it records the host, the version and the checksums hash, next to the approved keys.

The user's question, why a release would republish under the same tag, has its own reply: the finding "Releases get republished under the same tag after a failed or fixed release".

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Releases get republished under the same tag after a failed or fixed release
nodes.body:
Reply to the question in the answer "On upgrade the checksums file hash may change only together with a version bump...": why would a release republish under the same tag?

**My inference**, from common release practice, not from shipit incidents:
- A release job fails half way. The author deletes the release and runs GoReleaser again on the same tag. The archives get new timestamps, so new hashes.
- The author finds a bug just after the release, moves the tag to a fixed commit and releases again.
- An attacker with write access replaces the archives and the checksums file. This is the case the hard fail exists for.

shipit cannot tell the honest cases from the attack. So the hard fail is right. The honest author has a cheap way out: publish a new patch version.

**Fact.** GitHub now has immutable releases. Once published, the assets and the tag cannot change. A deleted immutable release cannot reuse its tag, even in a new repo with the same name. (docs.github.com/en/code-security/supply-chain-security/understanding-your-software-supply-chain/immutable-releases)

**My inference for shipit:** the author docs can recommend immutable releases. Then the hard fail never hits an honest author on GitHub. The official shipit plugins should turn it on.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: shipit plugin test: a conformance runner against a fake host is how authors test a plugin
nodes.body:
**Decided by the user**, in the comment "Conformance runner, not docs". This closes the fog "How a plugin author tests a plugin against shipit".

- The deliverable is a command, `shipit plugin test`. Docs alone are not enough.
- It runs the plugin against a fake host, with no real cloud account.
- It checks: the handshake, every required step (`validate`, `plan`, `apply`, `status`, `destroy`), the state blob round trip, step timeouts and a scrubbed environment.
- It fails loud: one clear error per broken check.
- Authors run it in their own CI. The maintainers never review plugin code to know that a plugin speaks the protocol.

**My inference:** the timeout check needs a defined timeout rule first. See the question "Who sets the time limit of a plugin step?".

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: The maintainers vouch for the shipit org plugins only; passing shipit plugin test is a self-reported bar
nodes.body:
**Decided by the user**, in the comment "We vouch for shipit/* only". This closes the fog "Who maintains and vouches for third-party plugins".

- The maintainers maintain and vouch for the plugins in the shipit GitHub org only. Nothing else.
- A third-party plugin is found through the GitHub topic `shipit-plugin`. It is protected by the numeric repo id in the lock file.
- The only bar that shipit publishes: the plugin passes `shipit plugin test`. The author reports this. Nobody checks it.

This fits the decisions "No hosted registry: a static list in the repo is the ceiling" and "No plugin list in v1: a GitHub topic for discovery, install by owner/repo only".

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Who sets the time limit of a plugin step?
nodes.body:
**Where we are.** The finding "Upload and remote command stay inside the SSH plugin's apply step; the protocol needs a step timeout instead" says SSH `apply` can run 30 minutes, and Hetzner adds about 3 minutes. The decision "shipit plugin test: a conformance runner against a fake host is how authors test a plugin" must check timeouts.

**The problem.** A plugin can hang. Example: a CI job runs `shipit deploy`, and `shipit-ssh apply` waits forever on a dead server. When does shipit stop it, and who picks that number?

**What hangs on it.**
- The handshake fields and the JSON Schema, which must hold for 2 years.
- What `shipit plugin test` checks.
- Whether a hung plugin blocks a CI runner for minutes or hours.

options.label: An idle limit, reset by each streamed line, plus a total limit in the user's config (recommended)
options.detail: shipit stops a step that prints nothing for 10 minutes. A user can set a total limit per provider. Cost: a plugin with a long silent command must print a progress line now and then; the docs and shipit plugin test must say so.

options.label: The plugin declares a limit per step in the handshake
options.detail: shipit uses the plugin's own number, for example 30 minutes for SSH apply. Cost: a hung plugin with a high number blocks CI for that long, and the user cannot change it.

options.label: One fixed total limit for every step
options.detail: For example 60 minutes, the same for all plugins. Cost: simple, but wrong both ways: too long for validate, maybe too short for a big upload.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: How does shipit stop a running plugin step when the user presses Ctrl-C, also on Windows?
nodes.body:
**Where we are.** The finding "Upload and remote command stay inside the SSH plugin's apply step; the protocol needs a step timeout instead" notes that cancel is not on the map yet. One plugin process runs per step (decision "One plugin process per step, a capabilities list in the handshake, state as an opaque blob"). Windows is a hard constraint.

**The problem.** On Unix, shipit can send the plugin an interrupt signal. On Windows, Go cannot send an interrupt to a child process: `Process.Signal(os.Interrupt)` is not implemented there, only kill (pkg.go.dev/os#Process.Signal). Example: a user presses Ctrl-C 5 minutes into a 30-minute SSH `apply` on Windows. What does the plugin see?

**What hangs on it.**
- A protocol rule that every plugin author must follow for 2 years.
- Whether a cancelled deploy can clean up.
- What `shipit plugin test` checks.

options.label: shipit closes the plugin's stdin, waits a grace time, then kills it (recommended)
options.detail: The protocol says: stdin closed means stop now and clean up. The same rule works on every OS. After a grace time, for example 10 seconds, shipit kills the process. Cost: plugins must keep reading stdin during a step, and shipit plugin test must check it.

options.label: shipit kills the plugin at once
options.detail: Simple and the same on every OS. Cost: a half-done apply leaves files or a half-provisioned Hetzner server behind, with no cleanup.

options.label: A signal on Unix, a console break event on Windows
options.detail: shipit sends an interrupt on Unix. On Windows it starts each plugin in its own process group and sends a break event. Cost: two code paths to keep for 2 years, and plugin authors must handle both.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Where does shipit read the version of a plugin installed from an HTTPS URL?
nodes.body:
**Where we are.** The decision "On upgrade, a new checksums hash needs a new version; a new URL host needs re-approval" lets the hash change only with a version bump. For a GitHub plugin, the release tag gives the version. A plain HTTPS URL has no tag.

**The problem.** Example: the lock entry says version 1.2.0 for `https://git.corp/acme/releases/v1.2/checksums.txt`. An upgrade gives `https://git.corp/acme/releases/latest/checksums.txt` with a new hash. shipit must know if this is 1.3.0 or a changed 1.2.0.

**What hangs on it.**
- Whether the version rule can work at all for URL plugins.
- Whether shipit runs any plugin code before an approval.
- The fields of a URL lock entry, which v1 must fix now.

options.label: The user passes the version on install and upgrade (recommended)
options.detail: For example shipit plugin install <url> --version 1.3.0. shipit stores it in the lock entry and runs nothing before the hash checks. Cost: one more flag to type, and a user can type a wrong number.

options.label: From the plugin's handshake, after the hash checks
options.detail: shipit downloads, checks the hashes, then runs the plugin once to ask its version. Cost: shipit runs new code before the user approves the upgrade, and the plugin reports its own version.

options.label: From the archive or checksums file name
options.detail: GoReleaser's default names hold the version, for example _1.3.0_. Cost: the goreleaser init style has no version in the archive name, and other tools differ.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Design doc draft: shipit v2 plugin system
nodes.body:
Reply to the comment "Draft the design doc now". This draft collects the decisions on the map. It adds no new choices. Each section names its source decisions. Three points are still open; the last section lists them.

# shipit v2 plugin system — draft

## 1. Why
14 open issues ask for new providers (Railway, Coolify, Dokku, internal platforms). Three volunteer maintainers cannot review and maintain provider code forever. **Test of the design:** new providers live and are maintained outside the shipit repo.

**Hard constraints:** one static binary (CGO_ENABLED=0); Windows works (about 20% of users); Homebrew, Scoop and `go install` keep working; the plugin API holds for 2 years or more. (Decision "Hard constraints: static binary, Windows support, current install paths, a 2-year API".)

## 2. Mechanism
- A plugin is a program named `shipit-<name>` on PATH (`.exe` on Windows), as with git and kubectl. Not go-plugin, not Go's `plugin` package, not WebAssembly.
- **One process per step.** shipit starts the plugin, writes one JSON request to stdin, reads one JSON result from stdout. A long step streams progress as one JSON line per event.
- **Handshake first.** The plugin reports: the protocol majors it speaks, its capabilities, the credential key names it needs, and whether it needs the real HOME.
- **State** is an opaque blob. The plugin returns it with a result, shipit passes it back to the next step unchanged. It lives in memory for one shipit command and never touches disk.
- We publish a JSON Schema for every message. The Schema allows unknown fields; both sides ignore them.

(Decisions "Plugins are programs on PATH named shipit-<name>, with a versioned JSON contract", "One plugin process per step, a capabilities list in the handshake, state as an opaque blob", "The state blob lives in memory for one shipit command and never touches disk".)

## 3. v1 API surface
| Step | In | Out |
|---|---|---|
| `validate` | config | ok or errors |
| `plan` | app | diff |
| `apply` | plan | streamed log lines, then the result |
| `status` | app | status |
| `destroy` | app | result |

All five are required. **Capability `secrets`:** secrets sync, optional, declared in the handshake (Fly and Render have it). Upload and remote command are not protocol steps: the SSH plugin does them inside `apply`. `status` and `destroy` need no blob. (Decision "v1 plugin API: five required steps, plus Secrets as a capability".)

## 4. Discovery and install
- **Discovery:** the GitHub topic `shipit-plugin`. The docs link to the topic search with a plain "not reviewed" note. No plugin list, no hosted registry, no infrastructure we run.
- **Install sources:** `shipit plugin install owner/repo` (GitHub release), or `shipit plugin install https://host/path/checksums.txt` (any HTTPS server; archives sit next to the file).
- **Archives:** shipit picks its OS and CPU from the names in the checksums file. It accepts both GoReleaser name styles, and `tar.gz` and `zip`. The author docs show only GoReleaser's built-in default.
- **Official plugins** live in the shipit GitHub org. shipit has a short built-in list of them and installs one on first use, with a notice and the lock line to commit.

(Decisions "No plugin list in v1: a GitHub topic for discovery, install by owner/repo only", "shipit plugin install accepts GitHub owner/repo or an HTTPS URL to a checksums file", "shipit accepts both GoReleaser archive name styles; the docs show only the built-in default", "Official plugins live in the shipit GitHub org; shipit installs them on first use and prints the lock line".)

## 5. The lock file
One project lock file, committed. Per plugin it holds: the source (owner/repo with its numeric repo id, or the URL host), the version, the sha256 of the release's checksums file, the approved key names, and the real-HOME approval.
- The lock file has a format version. shipit ignores lock fields it does not know, so a signer field can come later.
- **Hard fails, with no skip flag:** a different GitHub repo id; a different URL host; the same version with a different checksums hash; a new key name or a new real-HOME request on upgrade; any plugin with no lock entry in CI.

(Decisions "The lock file pins the sha256 of the release's checksums file", "The lock entry of a GitHub plugin records the numeric repo id; a different id is a hard fail", "On upgrade, a new checksums hash needs a new version; a new URL host needs re-approval"; finding "A signature check can come later without breaking the lock file, if v1 reserves room for it".)

## 6. Credentials and security stance
- shipit holds host credentials. It starts each plugin with a scrubbed environment: a small allow list (PATH, TEMP and the like) plus the plugin's approved keys only.
- The user approves the key names once; the approval lives in the lock file. CI reads it and never prompts. Key names matching `AWS_*`, `GOOGLE_*` or `AZURE_*` get a loud warning.
- Each plugin gets a private HOME (HOME, XDG_CONFIG_HOME, USERPROFILE, APPDATA, TMP). Real HOME only on approval.
- **What we promise, in these words:** "shipit gives a plugin only the secrets you approve for it." **What we do not promise:** that a plugin cannot read your files. A private HOME is hygiene, not a sandbox. Installing a plugin means trusting its author.
- No plugin starts another plugin in v1.

(Decisions "shipit holds credentials, scrubs the env, and passes each plugin only its declared keys", "Approved credential keys live in the project lock file, next to the pinned version and sha256", "Each plugin gets a private HOME by default; real HOME only on approval, and the docs call it hygiene, not a sandbox"; finding "Env scrubbing stops env-var theft but not file reads".)

## 7. Versioning and compatibility
- Within a protocol major: additions only. No removals, no renames, no silent behaviour changes.
- The handshake negotiates: shipit picks the highest major both sides speak.
- A protocol major stays supported for at least 2 years after its successor ships. New features, such as a long-lived session, come as capabilities, not majors.

(Decisions "Compatibility policy: additions only within a protocol major, a negotiated version, protocol N and N-1 both supported", "Protocol support: each protocol major stays supported for at least 2 years after its successor ships".)

## 8. Who vouches for what
The maintainers maintain and vouch for the shipit org plugins only. For third-party plugins, the only published bar is passing `shipit plugin test`, self-reported. (Decision "The maintainers vouch for the shipit org plugins only; passing shipit plugin test is a self-reported bar".)

## 9. Conformance runner: `shipit plugin test`
Runs a plugin against a fake host. Checks the handshake, all five steps, the state blob round trip, step timeouts and the scrubbed environment. Fails loud. Authors run it in their own CI. (Decision "shipit plugin test: a conformance runner against a fake host is how authors test a plugin".)

## 10. Migration plan
1. **SSH** moves first to `shipit/shipit-ssh`: no vendor API, but the longest `apply` (upload and remote command, up to 30 minutes).
2. **Hetzner** moves second to `shipit/shipit-hetzner`: a vendor API with a token, least used. It provisions a server, then uses the SSH code.
3. The SSH upload and remote command code moves to a shared Go module, `shipit-sdk`. Both plugins import it. Renovate handles the double releases.
4. Users keep `provider: ssh` or `provider: hetzner` in their config. shipit installs the official plugin on first use and prints the lock line. CI users commit that line.
5. **Fly** moves last, after the protocol has survived the two plugins above. **Render** has no slot yet.

(Decisions "SSH and Hetzner move out first; Fly moves last", "SSH upload and remote command move to a shared Go module, shipit-sdk; no plugin calls another plugin in v1".)

## 11. Open before implementation
- Step time limits: the question "Who sets the time limit of a plugin step?".
- Cancel on Ctrl-C, also on Windows: the question "How does shipit stop a running plugin step when the user presses Ctrl-C, also on Windows?".
- The version of a URL plugin: the question "Where does shipit read the version of a plugin installed from an HTTPS URL?".
- Smaller, not blocking: when Render moves; whether the Go sigstore verifier builds with CGO_ENABLED=0 (needed only when signatures come).

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Design a plugin system so third parties can add deploy providers to shipit
nodes.body:
## Destination
A design doc for shipit v2's plugin system. The three maintainers can implement it and commit to it for two years.

## Notes
- **shipit**: our open-source Go CLI. It deploys apps to cloud hosts.
- **Provider**: the code that talks to one host (Fly, Render, Hetzner, SSH). Today all providers are built into shipit.
- **Plugin**: a provider that is shipped and versioned outside the main repo.
- Standing preference: the maintainers are volunteers with little time.
- Standing preference: the main binary must stay simple to install.

## Done when
- The plugin mechanism is chosen.
- The discovery and install story is written.
- The v1 plugin API surface is listed.
- The versioning and compatibility policy is stated.
- The security stance on credentials is stated.
- Two built-in providers are planned as the first plugins, to prove the design.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Go CLIs load plugins in four known ways
nodes.body:
Go tools use four known ways to load code that ships outside the main binary.

1. **Separate program, called over RPC.** shipit starts the plugin as a child process and talks to it over gRPC. Terraform and Packer do this with HashiCorp's go-plugin library. Plugins can be in any language. Each call crosses a process boundary.
2. **Separate program on PATH, called once per command.** shipit runs `shipit-<name>` and passes data as JSON on stdin and stdout. git and kubectl find plugins this way. It is the simplest contract, but it has no long-lived session.
3. **Go's `plugin` package.** shipit loads a shared library into its own process. It works only on Linux, macOS and FreeBSD, not Windows. The plugin must be built with the same Go version and the same dependency versions as shipit. Thus each shipit release breaks every plugin.
4. **WebAssembly module.** shipit runs the plugin in an embedded runtime such as wazero. The plugin is sandboxed and portable. Network access and Go support inside WASM are still limited.

Sources: Go `plugin` package docs (pkg.go.dev/plugin, "Warnings" section); github.com/hashicorp/go-plugin README; kubectl plugin docs (kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/extend-kubectl/kubectl-plugins). The trade-off summary is my inference.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Which mechanism loads a plugin into shipit?
nodes.body:
**Where we are.** Today every provider (Fly, Render, Hetzner, SSH) is compiled into shipit. The finding "Go CLIs load plugins in four known ways" lists the options.

**The problem.** We must pick one way for shipit to run code that ships outside the main repo. The choice must stay stable for two years. It must keep the main binary simple to install, and it must be cheap for three volunteer maintainers to keep alive.

**What hangs on it.** How plugins are found and installed. The form of the v1 API (protobuf schema or JSON documents). What a plugin can reach on the user's machine, so the credential stance. How much work the first two plugins are.

options.label: Separate program over gRPC (recommended)
options.detail: shipit starts the plugin as a child process and calls it over gRPC, as Terraform does. A typed contract and a long-lived session. Cost: we take on go-plugin and protobuf, and authors must learn them.

options.label: Separate program on PATH, JSON over stdin/stdout
options.detail: shipit runs shipit-<name> once per step, as git and kubectl do. The simplest contract, any language. Cost: no typed schema, and we must version the JSON by hand.

options.label: WebAssembly module
options.detail: shipit runs the plugin in a sandbox inside its own process. Strong isolation and one file per plugin. Cost: weak network support in WASM today, and few authors know the toolchain.

options.label: Go plugin package
options.detail: shipit loads a shared library. Fast calls. Cost: no Windows, and every shipit release breaks every plugin. This conflicts with a two-year commitment.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Who holds the host credentials: shipit or the plugin?
nodes.body:
**Where we are.** Today each built-in provider reads its host's API token. There is one binary, so there is one trust boundary. With plugins, third-party code runs on the user's machine during a deploy.

**The problem.** A plugin needs a host token to deploy. For example, a Hetzner plugin needs a Hetzner API token. We must decide if shipit gives the plugin the token, or if the plugin finds it itself. A malicious or buggy plugin could leak any token it can read.

**What hangs on it.** Which credential calls are in the v1 API. What the design doc can promise users about third-party plugins. How much the first two plugins must change from today's code.

options.label: shipit holds them and passes each plugin only its own (recommended)
options.detail: shipit reads credentials from its config or env vars and hands a plugin only the keys declared for that provider. One place to audit. Cost: the API must carry credentials, and shipit must know each provider's key names.

options.label: Each plugin reads its own credentials
options.detail: The plugin reads env vars or the host's own config files itself, as the host's own CLI would. Least work for us. Cost: we cannot say what a third-party plugin reads, so our security story is 'trust the plugin'.

options.label: shipit holds them and signs requests for the plugin
options.detail: The plugin never sees a secret; it asks shipit to make authenticated calls. Strongest stance. Cost: shipit must know every host's auth scheme, which defeats the point of plugins.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Which two built-in providers move out first as plugins?
nodes.body:
**Where we are.** The goal says two built-in providers must become the first plugins, to prove the design. shipit has four built-ins: Fly, Render, Hetzner and SSH.

**The problem.** The two we pick decide how well the proof tests the API. A vendor API with a token (Fly, Render, Hetzner) is a different shape from a raw server over SSH. A pair of the same shape proves less.

**What hangs on it.** Which calls the v1 API must have. Which users see the move first and need a migration path.

options.label: SSH and Fly (recommended)
options.detail: SSH has no vendor API and tests long-running commands and file upload. Fly is a typical vendor API with a token. Together they cover both shapes. Cost: SSH is likely the most used provider, so a bug there hits many users.

options.label: Hetzner and Render
options.detail: Two vendor-API providers that fewer users depend on. A low-risk first move. Cost: they look alike, so the API may miss what SSH-style providers need.

options.label: Fly and Render
options.detail: The two most similar platform hosts. The fastest proof. Cost: the weakest test of the API's breadth.

nodes.title: Exec plugins on PATH (shipit-<name>), but with a real contract: versioned JSON messages, a handshake that reports protocol version, and a JSON Schema we publish. Not go-plugin: gRPC + protobuf is a lot to ask of someone writing a Coolify adapter on a weekend, and we'd be maintaining go-plugin's process mgmt too. Long-lived session — do we actually need one? Deploys are a handful of steps.
nodes.body: Fear with plain exec is no-contract chaos (every plugin invents its own flags). The contract is the part I care about, not the transport.

nodes.author: user
nodes.title: shipit holds them and passes each plugin only its own (recommended)
nodes.body: People run shipit in CI with cloud creds in env. A plugin that can read the whole env can exfiltrate AWS keys it has nothing to do with. So: shipit scrubs the env and passes only declared keys.

nodes.author: user
nodes.title: Real pain: we can't review provider PRs
nodes.body:
Context on why this exists. 14 open issues ask for new providers: Railway, Coolify, Dokku, and a few internal company platforms nobody outside can even test. Three of us, all volunteers, ~5h/week each. The bottleneck isn't the code, it's that every provider PR lands on us to review and then maintain forever.

Hard constraints, not preferences:
- shipit stays one static binary, CGO_ENABLED=0.
- Windows is ~20% of users. Anything that doesn't work on Windows is out.
- Install paths are Homebrew, Scoop and `go install`. Plugins can't break those.
- Whatever API we ship has to hold for 2+ years. We broke people in v0.x and I'm not doing that again.

nodes.author: user
nodes.title: No registry we have to run
nodes.body: I don't want to run infra. No server, no signing service, no uptime we're on the hook for. A static list in the repo (a markdown file or a JSON index on GitHub) is about the ceiling of what we can maintain. Is "listed" even an endorsement though? Users will read it as one.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Plugins are programs on PATH named shipit-<name>, with a versioned JSON contract
nodes.body:
**Decided by the user.** shipit finds a plugin as a program named `shipit-<name>` on PATH, as git and kubectl do. It is not go-plugin: gRPC and protobuf ask too much of a weekend author, and we do not want to maintain process management.

The transport is simple. The contract is the part that matters:
- Every message is a JSON document with a protocol version in it.
- A handshake comes first. The plugin reports the protocol versions it speaks.
- We publish a JSON Schema for every message. Plugins do not invent their own flags.

This fits the hard constraints: no CGO, works on Windows (Go's `exec.LookPath` also finds `shipit-<name>.exe`), and the main binary stays one static file.

Still open: whether one plugin process lives for one step or for a whole deploy. See the question "Does a plugin process live for one step or for one whole deploy?".

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: shipit holds credentials, scrubs the env, and passes each plugin only its declared keys
nodes.body:
**Decided by the user.** shipit reads host credentials from its config or the environment. When it starts a plugin, it gives the plugin a cleaned environment that holds only the keys declared for that plugin.

Reason: people run shipit in CI with cloud credentials in the environment. A plugin that can read the whole environment can steal AWS keys that it has nothing to do with.

Consequences for the v1 API:
- A plugin must declare its key names somewhere shipit can read before it runs the plugin.
- shipit needs a small allow list of safe variables to keep (for example PATH, HOME, TEMP on Windows), else plugins break.

Still open: who approves the declared keys. See the question "Who approves the credential keys a plugin declares?".

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Env scrubbing stops env-var theft but not file reads
nodes.body:
**My inference**, from how exec plugins work (finding "Go CLIs load plugins in four known ways").

A plugin is a normal program. It runs with all the rights of the user who runs shipit. A clean environment stops it from reading AWS keys in env vars. It does not stop it from reading `~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, or a CI runner's files, or from opening a network connection.

So the design doc can promise: "shipit gives a plugin only the secrets you declare for it." It cannot promise: "a plugin cannot read your other secrets." Installing a plugin is trusting its author, as with a git or kubectl plugin. The doc must say this in plain words.

A real sandbox would need the WebAssembly option, which the user did not pick.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Does a plugin process live for one step or for one whole deploy?
nodes.body:
**Where we are.** The decision "Plugins are programs on PATH named shipit-<name>, with a versioned JSON contract" fixes the transport. The user asked if a long-lived session is needed, since a deploy is only a few steps.

**The problem.** shipit can start the plugin once per step (validate, deploy, status, logs) or once for the whole deploy. My inference: one run per step is enough for a few steps. Two cases need care. Logs and long deploys need streaming output, which one run can do with one JSON line per event. A step that needs the result of an earlier step needs shipit to pass that state back in.

**What hangs on it.** The message shapes in the JSON Schema. How a plugin author tests by hand (pipe a file into the program, or not). How shipit handles timeouts and Ctrl-C on Windows.

options.label: One process per step (recommended)
options.detail: shipit runs shipit-fly once for validate, once for deploy, and so on. Each run reads one JSON request on stdin and writes one JSON result on stdout. A long step streams progress as one JSON line per event. Simplest for authors and easy to test by hand. Cost: state between steps (for example a release id) must go back through shipit.

options.label: One process per deploy
options.detail: shipit starts the plugin once and sends it a sequence of JSON messages over stdin and stdout. The plugin keeps state in memory. Cost: authors must write a message loop, and shipit must handle a plugin that hangs or dies mid-deploy.

options.label: Per step now, session as a later protocol version
options.detail: Ship one process per step in protocol v1. Keep room in the handshake to add a session mode in v2 if a provider needs it. Cost: a second mode to support later, if it comes.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Who approves the credential keys a plugin declares?
nodes.body:
**Where we are.** The decision "shipit holds credentials, scrubs the env, and passes each plugin only its declared keys" is settled. Somebody must say which keys belong to which plugin.

**The problem.** If the plugin alone says which keys it needs, a bad plugin can ask for the AWS keys too. For example, a "Coolify" plugin could declare COOLIFY_TOKEN and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY. Someone must check that list.

**What hangs on it.** A handshake field for key names. A first-run prompt, and how CI skips it. What the design doc can promise users.

options.label: The plugin declares, the user confirms once (recommended)
options.detail: The handshake lists the key names, for example FLY_API_TOKEN. On first use, shipit shows the list and asks the user to confirm. In CI, a flag or the project config confirms it. Cost: one prompt, and a place to store the approval.

options.label: The user lists keys per plugin in the project config
options.detail: The plugin declares nothing. The shipit config says which env vars each plugin gets. Most explicit. Cost: every user must write config before the first deploy.

options.label: The plugin declares, shipit trusts it
options.detail: shipit passes whatever keys the handshake lists. No prompt. Cost: a bad plugin can just declare AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, so the scrubbing protects little.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Hard constraints: static binary, Windows support, current install paths, a 2-year API
nodes.body:
**Stated by the user as hard constraints, not preferences.**
- shipit stays one static binary, built with CGO_ENABLED=0.
- Windows is about 20% of users. A design that does not work on Windows is out.
- shipit installs through Homebrew, Scoop and `go install`. Plugins must not break these paths.
- The plugin API must hold for 2 years or more. No breaking changes like in v0.x.

**Why the plugin system exists.** 14 open issues ask for new providers (Railway, Coolify, Dokku, internal company platforms). Three volunteer maintainers have about 5 hours a week each. The cost is not the code. It is that every provider PR lands on them to review and maintain forever. So the main test of the design: new providers live and are maintained outside the shipit repo.

Effect on earlier options: Go's `plugin` package is out (no Windows, needs CGO). The chosen exec-on-PATH mechanism meets all four constraints.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: No hosted registry: a static list in the repo is the ceiling
nodes.body:
**Stated by the user.** The maintainers run no infrastructure for plugins: no server, no signing service, nothing with uptime. The most they keep is a static list in the shipit repo, as a markdown file or a JSON index on GitHub.

Still open: whether such a list exists, and what being on it means. See the question "What does a listing in the shipit plugin list promise?".

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Users read any plugin list as an endorsement, even with a disclaimer
nodes.body:
**Where this comes from.** The comment "No registry we have to run" asked: does a listing in a shipit plugin list mean the maintainers endorse the plugin?

**Prior art.**
- GitHub CLI keeps no list. Authors tag their repo with the GitHub topic `gh-extension`. Users search that topic. `gh extension install owner/gh-name` installs from the repo's releases. (cli.github.com/manual/gh_extension_install)
- Krew, the kubectl plugin manager, keeps one central index repo. The maintainers admit plugins "on a case-by-case basis". A rejected author can host an own index. (github.com/kubernetes-sigs/krew-index README)

**My inference.**
- Users read "listed" as "the maintainers checked this". A disclaimer in the docs does not change that much.
- A list that the maintainers keep means pull requests to the list. That is review work again: the cost in "Real pain: we can't review provider PRs".
- A GitHub topic costs the maintainers nothing and implies no endorsement.
- If a list exists, the honest version says exactly what was checked, for example "the handshake passes", and nothing more.

history.title: Users read a list as an endorsement unless it says otherwise
history.body:
Answer to "Is listed even an endorsement?" in the comment "No registry we have to run".

**Prior art.**
- GitHub CLI keeps no list at all. Authors tag a repo with the GitHub topic `gh-extension`, and users search the topic. `gh extension install owner/gh-name` installs from the repo's releases. Its docs carry no trust warning. (cli.github.com/manual/gh_extension_install)
- kubectl's Krew keeps one central index repo of plugin manifests. Admission is decided "on a case-by-case basis". A rejected author can host a custom index. (github.com/kubernetes-sigs/krew-index README)

**My inference.** Yes, users read "listed" as "the maintainers checked this", whatever the doc says. A list written by the maintainers also means PRs to the list, which is again review work, the cost in "Real pain: we can't review provider PRs". A GitHub topic costs the maintainers nothing and implies no endorsement. If there is a list, the honest version says what was checked (for example "the handshake passes") and nothing more.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: What does a listing in the shipit plugin list promise?
nodes.body:
**Where we are.** The decision "No hosted registry: a static list in the repo is the ceiling" sets the upper limit. The finding "Users read a list as an endorsement unless it says otherwise" shows that users treat a list as a promise.

**The problem.** We must choose between no list, a list with a disclaimer, a list with an automated check, or a reviewed list. Each makes a different promise to users and costs the maintainers different work.

**What hangs on it.** The `shipit plugin install` story (install by short name needs an index; install by owner/repo does not). What the design doc says about trust. How much work lands on the three maintainers.

options.label: No list: a GitHub topic only (recommended)
options.detail: Authors tag their repo shipit-plugin. The docs link to the topic search. Zero review work, and no implied endorsement. Cost: users find plugins less easily, and look-alike or abandoned plugins sit next to good ones.

options.label: A list anyone can join, with a clear disclaimer
options.detail: A JSON file in the repo. A CI job merges an entry if the manifest is valid. The file and docs say 'not reviewed, use at your own risk'. Cost: PRs to the list still need a click, and users may still read it as an endorsement.

options.label: A list with an automated check
options.detail: As above, but CI also runs the plugin's handshake against the published JSON Schema. The listing promises only 'speaks the protocol'. Cost: a CI job to keep alive, and it needs the plugin binaries.

options.label: A small reviewed list
options.detail: The maintainers review each listed plugin. Users get real trust. Cost: exactly the review work this plugin system exists to remove.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Exec-plugin CLIs install plugins from GitHub releases or a git index
nodes.body:
Research for "How users find and install plugins", for programs on PATH (decision "Plugins are programs on PATH named shipit-<name>, with a versioned JSON contract").

**Prior art.**
1. **git and kubectl alone**: no install command. The user puts `git-foo` or `kubectl-foo` on PATH by any means, for example Homebrew or Scoop. (kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/extend-kubectl/kubectl-plugins)
2. **GitHub CLI**: `gh extension install owner/gh-name`. It first looks for prebuilt binaries in the repo's GitHub release. If there is no release, it clones the repo and expects a script at the root. On Windows it uses an equivalent of a symlink. No index; discovery is the GitHub topic `gh-extension`. (cli.github.com/manual/gh_extension_install)
3. **Krew for kubectl**: a git repo of YAML manifests. Each manifest gives, per OS and CPU, an archive URL and its sha256. `kubectl krew install name` reads the index and checks the hash. (krew.sigs.k8s.io/docs/developer-guide/plugin-manifest; github.com/kubernetes-sigs/krew-index)

**My inference for shipit.**
- The gh model fits the constraints best: no infrastructure, no Go toolchain for the user, works on Windows. Authors publish binaries with GitHub releases (for example with GoReleaser).
- A command such as `shipit plugin install owner/shipit-coolify` can download into a shipit plugin directory and pin the version and sha256 in a project lock file. This also helps CI.
- Install by short name (`shipit plugin install coolify`) needs an index. That depends on the question "What does a listing in the shipit plugin list promise?".
- Authors can still ship through Homebrew or Scoop, since plain PATH lookup keeps working.

Not checked: Helm and Terraform. Terraform's registry is hosted infrastructure, which the decision "No hosted registry: a static list in the repo is the ceiling" rules out.

nodes.author: user
nodes.title: Per step now, session as a later protocol version
nodes.body: Per step, yes. But the handshake gets a capabilities list from day one, so a v2 session mode is an addition, not a break. State between steps goes back through shipit as an opaque blob the plugin owns — shipit never parses it.

nodes.author: user
nodes.title: Plugin declares key names in the handshake; user confirms once. Approval lives in the lock file next to the pinned version + sha256, so CI just reads the committed lock — no prompt, no extra flag. New key on upgrade = lock mismatch = hard fail until someone re-approves. Anything matching AWS_*/GOOGLE_*/AZURE_* gets a loud warning in the prompt.

nodes.author: user
nodes.title: No list: a GitHub topic only (recommended)
nodes.body: Topic only for v1. If a list happens later it's option 2 (speaks the protocol), never a reviewed one. Install is owner/repo, no short names.

nodes.author: user
nodes.title: Fake HOME per plugin — worth it?
nodes.body: Cheap extra layer, or theatre? shipit could start each plugin with HOME, XDG_CONFIG_HOME and TMP pointed at a per-plugin dir under the shipit cache. Doesn't stop a plugin that hardcodes /home/runner/.aws, but kills the lazy `os.UserHomeDir()` + read ~/.aws path. Works on Windows too (USERPROFILE/APPDATA). Worth it, or does it just break plugins that legitimately shell out to ssh/git with the user's config?

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: One plugin process per step, a capabilities list in the handshake, state as an opaque blob
nodes.body:
**Decided by the user**, in the answer to "Does a plugin process live for one step or for one whole deploy?".

- **Protocol v1 runs one process per step.** shipit starts `shipit-<name>` once for each step (for example validate, deploy, status, logs). Each run reads one JSON request and writes one JSON result. A long step streams progress as one JSON line per event.
- **The handshake has a capabilities list from day one.** The plugin lists the features it supports. A session mode in v2 becomes a new capability, not a breaking change. Old plugins that do not list it keep working.
- **State between steps is an opaque blob.** The plugin returns a blob with a step result. shipit passes it back unchanged to the next step. shipit never reads or parses it. The plugin owns its format.

Still open: how long shipit keeps the blob. See the question "Does the state blob outlive one shipit command?".

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Approved credential keys live in the project lock file, next to the pinned version and sha256
nodes.body:
**Decided by the user**, in the answer to "Who approves the credential keys a plugin declares?".

- The plugin declares its key names in the handshake, for example `FLY_API_TOKEN`.
- On first use, shipit shows the list. The user confirms it once.
- shipit writes the approval into the project lock file. The lock file holds, per plugin: the pinned version, its sha256, and the approved key names.
- CI reads the committed lock file. There is no prompt and no extra flag in CI.
- On upgrade, a new key name makes the lock file not match. shipit then stops with an error until somebody approves again.
- Key names that match `AWS_*`, `GOOGLE_*` or `AZURE_*` get a loud warning in the prompt.

**My inference**, not stated by the user: a plugin with no entry in the lock file also stops with an error in CI. CI never approves keys itself.

Still open: what the sha256 pins when one lock file serves Windows, macOS and Linux. See the question "Which sha256 does the lock file pin for a plugin built for many platforms?".

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: No plugin list in v1: a GitHub topic for discovery, install by owner/repo only
nodes.body:
**Decided by the user**, in the answer to "What does a listing in the shipit plugin list promise?".

- **v1 has no plugin list.** Authors tag their repo with the GitHub topic `shipit-plugin`. The shipit docs link to the topic search.
- **Install takes owner/repo**, for example `shipit plugin install acme/shipit-coolify`. There are no short names, so shipit needs no index.
- **A later list, if any, only says "speaks the protocol".** CI would check the plugin's handshake against the published JSON Schema. The maintainers never keep a reviewed list.

This lowers the ceiling in the decision "No hosted registry: a static list in the repo is the ceiling": for v1, not even the static list exists.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: A private HOME per plugin breaks provider CLIs that keep their login in HOME, and does not hide SSH keys
nodes.body:
Answer to the comment "Fake HOME per plugin — worth it?".

**Facts.**
- Go's `os.UserHomeDir` returns `$HOME` on Unix and `%USERPROFILE%` on Windows. `os.UserConfigDir` uses `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` or `%AppData%`. So a private HOME does redirect the lazy path in a Go plugin. (pkg.go.dev/os#UserHomeDir)
- git reads `$HOME/.gitconfig` and `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/git/config`. With a private HOME, git loses the user's identity, credential helpers and `url.insteadOf` rules. (git-scm.com/docs/git-config, section FILES)
- OpenSSH finds `~/.ssh` from the user's password-database entry, not from `$HOME`. So `ssh` and `git push` over SSH still read the real keys. A private HOME does not hide SSH keys from a plugin that runs `ssh`. (OpenSSH source, ssh.c: home directory from `getpwuid`)
- Many provider CLIs keep their login token in HOME: flyctl in `~/.fly/config.yml`, Docker in `~/.docker/config.json`, kubectl in `~/.kube/config`.

**My inference.**
- A private TMP per plugin is cheap and breaks nothing. Keep it.
- A private HOME helps against a lazy or careless plugin. It does nothing against a hostile one, as the finding "Env scrubbing stops env-var theft but not file reads" says.
- It breaks a common, legitimate case: a plugin that wraps the provider's own CLI and relies on the user's `fly auth login` or `docker login`. Dokku-style plugins that `git push` lose git config but keep SSH.
- Best fit with what is settled: private HOME by default, and a plugin that needs the real HOME says so in the handshake. The approval goes into the lock file, like credential keys. Then "this plugin reads your home directory" is visible in review.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Does shipit give each plugin a private HOME?
nodes.body:
**Where we are.** shipit gives each plugin a clean environment with only its approved keys (decision "shipit holds credentials, scrubs the env, and passes each plugin only its declared keys"). Files in the user's home directory stay readable. The finding "A private HOME per plugin breaks provider CLIs that keep their login in HOME, and does not hide SSH keys" weighs a private HOME.

**The problem.** A private HOME stops a careless plugin from reading `~/.aws`. It also breaks a plugin that runs `flyctl` or `docker` and relies on the user's saved login. Example: a `shipit-fly` that calls `flyctl deploy` fails with "not logged in".

**What hangs on it.** A handshake field and a lock-file field, or neither. What the design doc promises about files. How plugin authors pass provider logins.

Why not "private HOME by default" without the approval? Then authors who need HOME have no way to get it.

options.label: Private HOME by default, real HOME on approval (recommended)
options.detail: shipit points HOME, XDG_CONFIG_HOME, USERPROFILE, APPDATA and TMP at a per-plugin directory. A plugin that needs the real HOME declares it in the handshake, and the user approves it once in the lock file. Cost: one more handshake field and lock entry; authors who wrap flyctl or docker must declare it.

options.label: Private TMP only, real HOME always
options.detail: Each plugin gets its own temp directory. HOME stays real. Nothing breaks. Cost: a careless plugin can read ~/.aws with os.UserHomeDir; only the trust warning in the docs protects users.

options.label: Private HOME always, no way out
options.detail: Every plugin gets a private HOME. Cost: plugins that wrap a provider CLI must pass tokens as declared keys instead of using the CLI's saved login, and some will not work at all.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Does the state blob outlive one shipit command?
nodes.body:
**Where we are.** The decision "One plugin process per step, a capabilities list in the handshake, state as an opaque blob" says shipit passes the plugin's blob from one step to the next. shipit never reads it.

**The problem.** Inside one `shipit deploy`, shipit can hold the blob in memory. But `shipit status` or `shipit logs` often runs later, as a new command, maybe on another machine. Example: the deploy step returns a Fly release id in the blob. Ten minutes later, `shipit logs` needs that id.

**What hangs on it.** The message shapes for status and logs in the JSON Schema. Whether shipit writes any state to disk. What a plugin must do when no blob comes in.

A later protocol version can add saved state as a capability, so the simplest choice now does not block it.

options.label: Only for one command (recommended)
options.detail: shipit keeps the blob in memory while one shipit deploy runs, and drops it after. A later shipit status or shipit logs gets no blob; the plugin finds the release from the provider or from an id the user passes. Cost: status and logs plugins do a little more lookup work.

options.label: Saved in a per-project cache outside the repo
options.detail: shipit saves the last blob per plugin in the user's cache directory. Later commands on the same machine get it. Cost: on a fresh CI runner the cache is empty, so plugins must handle a missing blob anyway.

options.label: Saved in a file in the project
options.detail: shipit writes the blob to a file under the project, for example .shipit/state. Cost: users commit it or ignore it, and an opaque blob can hold secrets that end up in git.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Which sha256 does the lock file pin for a plugin built for many platforms?
nodes.body:
**Where we are.** The decision "Approved credential keys live in the project lock file, next to the pinned version and sha256" says the committed lock file pins each plugin. CI reads it with no prompt.

**The problem.** A plugin release has one binary per OS and CPU. Each binary has its own sha256. About 20% of users are on Windows, and CI mostly runs on Linux. Example: a developer approves `acme/shipit-coolify` on a Mac. CI on Linux downloads a different file, so a single Mac hash does not match.

**What hangs on it.** The lock file format. What a plugin release must contain, for example a fixed asset name pattern or a checksums file. Whether `shipit plugin install` works offline from the lock file.

Prior art: Krew manifests list an archive URL and a sha256 per OS and CPU (finding "Exec-plugin CLIs install plugins from GitHub releases or a git index").

options.label: One sha256 per platform, all written at approval (recommended)
options.detail: On approval, shipit records the hash of every platform binary in the release, from the release's checksums file or by downloading each one. A Linux CI runner then finds its hash in a lock file made on a Mac. Cost: the approval step does more downloads, and releases need a fixed asset naming scheme.

options.label: Pin the release's checksums file
options.detail: The lock file holds one sha256: the hash of checksums.txt in the release. shipit checks each binary against that file. Cost: every plugin release must ship a checksums file, for example with GoReleaser.

options.label: One sha256, for the platform that approved
options.detail: The lock file holds only the hash of the binary that the approving user downloaded. Cost: CI on another OS finds no hash and stops, which breaks the CI story in the decision on approved keys.

nodes.title: The lock file pins the sha256 of the release's checksums file
nodes.body:
**Decided by the user**, in the answer to "Which sha256 does the lock file pin for a plugin built for many platforms?".

- Each plugin entry in the lock file holds one sha256: the hash of the release's checksums file (`checksums.txt`).
- On install, shipit downloads the checksums file, checks it against the pinned hash, then checks the binary for this OS and CPU against the line in that file.
- One lock file made on a Mac thus works on a Linux or Windows CI runner.
- **Rule for authors:** every plugin release must ship a checksums file. GoReleaser writes one by default, so most Go authors do nothing extra.

The user's follow-up on signatures has its own reply: the finding "A signature check can come later without breaking the lock file, if v1 reserves room for it".

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: A signature check can come later without breaking the lock file, if v1 reserves room for it
nodes.body:
Reply to the question in the answer "Pin the release's checksums file": can shipit require a cosign signature later without a lock format break?

**Fact.** GoReleaser can sign only the checksums file with cosign. Its documented setup runs `cosign sign-blob --bundle=checksums.txt.sigstore.json checksums.txt` on the `checksum` artifact. The release then holds one extra file, the signature bundle. Users verify the checksums file against the publisher's identity and OIDC issuer, then check each binary against the signed checksums. (goreleaser.com/customization/sign)

**My inference for shipit.**
- The signature signs the same file the lock file already pins. So signing adds to the lock entry, and changes nothing that is there.
- A later lock entry would add one field: the expected signer, for example the GitHub Actions workflow of `acme/shipit-coolify`. Keyless signing has no key to store.
- This is not a break only if v1 does two things now: the lock file has a format version number, and shipit ignores lock fields it does not know. Without these, an old shipit fails on a lock file that a new shipit wrote.
- Making the signature **required** is a later policy choice. It would break releases with no signature, so it needs a new lock format version, or it applies only to new entries.
- Not checked: whether the Go library for sigstore verification builds with CGO_ENABLED=0, as the hard constraints need.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Compatibility policy: additions only within a protocol major, a negotiated version, protocol N and N-1 both supported
nodes.body:
**Decided by the user**, in the comment "We broke users twice in 0.x; protocol N and N-1 both supported".

**Why.** shipit 0.x broke the provider config format twice, in 0.7 and in 0.11. People still pin 0.6 in CI because of it. v2 must not repeat that.

**The policy.**
- **Within one protocol major, changes are additions only.** New optional fields, new messages and new capabilities. Nothing is removed or renamed.
- **No silent behaviour changes in a minor.** The same request gives the same meaning in every minor of a major.
- **The handshake negotiates the version.** The plugin lists the protocol majors it speaks. shipit picks the highest one that both sides speak.
- **shipit supports protocol N and N-1**, for at least the 2-year commitment.

**My inference**, not stated by the user: additions only work if both sides ignore fields they do not know. The JSON Schema must allow unknown fields, and the docs must tell authors to ignore them.

Still open: what "N and N-1 for 2 years" means when a new major ships. See the question "When shipit adds protocol N+1, how long does N-1 stay supported?".

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: When shipit adds protocol N+1, how long does N-1 stay supported?
nodes.body:
**Where we are.** The decision "Compatibility policy: additions only within a protocol major, a negotiated version, protocol N and N-1 both supported" says shipit supports N and N-1 for at least 2 years.

**The problem.** "N and N-1" and "2 years" can conflict. Example: protocol 1 ships in 2027. Protocol 2 ships in 2028, protocol 3 in 2029. Under a strict N and N-1 window, protocol 1 plugins stop working in 2029, after only 2 years. A plugin written for protocol 2 in late 2028 gets only one year.

**What hangs on it.** The promise the design doc makes to plugin authors. How many protocol versions shipit's code must carry. What shipit prints when a plugin speaks only a dropped version.

options.label: Each major lives at least 2 years after its successor ships (recommended)
options.detail: shipit drops protocol N-1 only when N+1 exists AND N has been out for 2 years. A plugin author gets a fixed 2-year window, whatever happens. Cost: if majors come fast, shipit carries three protocols for a while.

options.label: Strict window: only N and N-1, at any time
options.detail: When N+1 ships, N-1 is dropped at once. shipit carries at most two protocols. Cost: two majors within a year break plugins that are only months old, which is the 0.x pain again.

options.label: At most one new protocol major every 2 years
options.detail: The maintainers promise not to ship a major sooner. Then the strict window also gives 2 years. Cost: an urgent breaking fix, for example a security hole in a message, must wait or break the promise.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: If install by owner/repo fails, it fails through renamed repos, typo names and a list that others write
nodes.body:
**My inference**, not checked against real incidents for shipit. Assume the decision "No plugin list in v1: a GitHub topic for discovery, install by owner/repo only" was chosen and failed a year later. The strongest reasons:

1. **A repo name changes owner.** GitHub redirects a renamed or transferred repo from the old name. If somebody later takes the old owner name, the old owner/repo can point at their code. An upgrade then pulls a release from a stranger. The pinned checksums hash stops this only until somebody approves the upgrade.
2. **Typo names.** `acme/shipit-coolify` and `acrne/shipit-coolify` look the same in a README. With no list, nothing tells users which one is real.
3. **Somebody else writes the list.** A GitHub topic is hard to browse and anybody can tag a repo. A community "awesome-shipit" page appears, and users read it as the maintainers' endorsement anyway (finding "Users read any plugin list as an endorsement, even with a disclaimer").
4. **Plugins on other hosts are left out.** Company platforms, one of the reasons for the plugin system (decision "Hard constraints: static binary, Windows support, current install paths, a 2-year API"), often live on GitLab or an internal server. owner/repo assumes GitHub.

**Cheap fixes inside the decision.** The lock entry can record the repo's numeric GitHub id, which does not move with the name. An upgrade whose id differs then stops with an error. The topic search link in the docs can carry a plain "not reviewed" warning.

**The strongest alternative.** Keep owner/repo for GitHub, and also accept a plain HTTPS URL to a release's checksums file. This serves internal platforms with no index and no list. The question "Does shipit plugin install accept sources other than GitHub releases?" offers it.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Design a plugin system so third parties can add deploy providers to shipit
nodes.body:
## Destination
A design doc for shipit v2's plugin system. The three maintainers can implement it and commit to it for two years.

## Notes
- **shipit**: our open-source Go CLI. It deploys apps to cloud hosts.
- **Provider**: the code that talks to one host (Fly, Render, Hetzner, SSH). Today all providers are built into shipit.
- **Plugin**: a provider that is shipped and versioned outside the main repo.
- Standing preference: the maintainers are volunteers with little time.
- Standing preference: the main binary must stay simple to install.

## Done when
- The plugin mechanism is chosen.
- The discovery and install story is written.
- The v1 plugin API surface is listed.
- The versioning and compatibility policy is stated.
- The security stance on credentials is stated.
- Two built-in providers are planned as the first plugins, to prove the design.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Go CLIs load plugins in four known ways
nodes.body:
Go tools use four known ways to load code that ships outside the main binary.

1. **Separate program, called over RPC.** shipit starts the plugin as a child process and talks to it over gRPC. Terraform and Packer do this with HashiCorp's go-plugin library. Plugins can be in any language. Each call crosses a process boundary.
2. **Separate program on PATH, called once per command.** shipit runs `shipit-<name>` and passes data as JSON on stdin and stdout. git and kubectl find plugins this way. It is the simplest contract, but it has no long-lived session.
3. **Go's `plugin` package.** shipit loads a shared library into its own process. It works only on Linux, macOS and FreeBSD, not Windows. The plugin must be built with the same Go version and the same dependency versions as shipit. Thus each shipit release breaks every plugin.
4. **WebAssembly module.** shipit runs the plugin in an embedded runtime such as wazero. The plugin is sandboxed and portable. Network access and Go support inside WASM are still limited.

Sources: Go `plugin` package docs (pkg.go.dev/plugin, "Warnings" section); github.com/hashicorp/go-plugin README; kubectl plugin docs (kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/extend-kubectl/kubectl-plugins). The trade-off summary is my inference.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Which mechanism loads a plugin into shipit?
nodes.body:
**Where we are.** Today every provider (Fly, Render, Hetzner, SSH) is compiled into shipit. The finding "Go CLIs load plugins in four known ways" lists the options.

**The problem.** We must pick one way for shipit to run code that ships outside the main repo. The choice must stay stable for two years. It must keep the main binary simple to install, and it must be cheap for three volunteer maintainers to keep alive.

**What hangs on it.** How plugins are found and installed. The form of the v1 API (protobuf schema or JSON documents). What a plugin can reach on the user's machine, so the credential stance. How much work the first two plugins are.

options.label: Separate program over gRPC (recommended)
options.detail: shipit starts the plugin as a child process and calls it over gRPC, as Terraform does. A typed contract and a long-lived session. Cost: we take on go-plugin and protobuf, and authors must learn them.

options.label: Separate program on PATH, JSON over stdin/stdout
options.detail: shipit runs shipit-<name> once per step, as git and kubectl do. The simplest contract, any language. Cost: no typed schema, and we must version the JSON by hand.

options.label: WebAssembly module
options.detail: shipit runs the plugin in a sandbox inside its own process. Strong isolation and one file per plugin. Cost: weak network support in WASM today, and few authors know the toolchain.

options.label: Go plugin package
options.detail: shipit loads a shared library. Fast calls. Cost: no Windows, and every shipit release breaks every plugin. This conflicts with a two-year commitment.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Who holds the host credentials: shipit or the plugin?
nodes.body:
**Where we are.** Today each built-in provider reads its host's API token. There is one binary, so there is one trust boundary. With plugins, third-party code runs on the user's machine during a deploy.

**The problem.** A plugin needs a host token to deploy. For example, a Hetzner plugin needs a Hetzner API token. We must decide if shipit gives the plugin the token, or if the plugin finds it itself. A malicious or buggy plugin could leak any token it can read.

**What hangs on it.** Which credential calls are in the v1 API. What the design doc can promise users about third-party plugins. How much the first two plugins must change from today's code.

options.label: shipit holds them and passes each plugin only its own (recommended)
options.detail: shipit reads credentials from its config or env vars and hands a plugin only the keys declared for that provider. One place to audit. Cost: the API must carry credentials, and shipit must know each provider's key names.

options.label: Each plugin reads its own credentials
options.detail: The plugin reads env vars or the host's own config files itself, as the host's own CLI would. Least work for us. Cost: we cannot say what a third-party plugin reads, so our security story is 'trust the plugin'.

options.label: shipit holds them and signs requests for the plugin
options.detail: The plugin never sees a secret; it asks shipit to make authenticated calls. Strongest stance. Cost: shipit must know every host's auth scheme, which defeats the point of plugins.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Which two built-in providers move out first as plugins?
nodes.body:
**Where we are.** The goal says two built-in providers must become the first plugins, to prove the design. shipit has four built-ins: Fly, Render, Hetzner and SSH.

**The problem.** The two we pick decide how well the proof tests the API. A vendor API with a token (Fly, Render, Hetzner) is a different shape from a raw server over SSH. A pair of the same shape proves less.

**What hangs on it.** Which calls the v1 API must have. Which users see the move first and need a migration path.

options.label: SSH and Fly (recommended)
options.detail: SSH has no vendor API and tests long-running commands and file upload. Fly is a typical vendor API with a token. Together they cover both shapes. Cost: SSH is likely the most used provider, so a bug there hits many users.

options.label: Hetzner and Render
options.detail: Two vendor-API providers that fewer users depend on. A low-risk first move. Cost: they look alike, so the API may miss what SSH-style providers need.

options.label: Fly and Render
options.detail: The two most similar platform hosts. The fastest proof. Cost: the weakest test of the API's breadth.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: List what today's built-in providers do, as input to the v1 API
nodes.body:
Read the shipit source. For each of Fly, Render, Hetzner and SSH, list the operations it does: for example validate config, build, upload, deploy, status, logs, rollback, destroy.

Mark which operations all four share and which only some have. The shared set is the first draft of the v1 plugin API surface. Note the Go interface (if any) that the providers implement today.

The user can do this, or point me at the shipit repo so I can do it.
